## Goals

- Practice core R syntax: functions, control flow, data frames
- Import data from `.csv` and inspect it before doing anything else
- Practice core `dplyr` verbs and reshape data with `pivot_longer()`/`pivot_wider()`

## Setup



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
```
:::



## Part 1: R fundamentals

### Functions and control flow



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wing_length <- c(23.1, 25.4, 22.8, 26.0, 24.3)
species <- c("A", "A", "B", "B", "B")

classify_size <- function(x, threshold = 24) {
  if (x > threshold) {
    "large"
  } else {
    "small"
  }
}

sapply(wing_length, classify_size)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "small" "large" "small" "large" "large"
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# A simple loop (you'll rarely need this once you know vectorized ops,
# but it's worth understanding)
for (i in seq_along(wing_length)) {
  cat(species[i], "-", wing_length[i], "\n")
}
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
A - 23.1 
A - 25.4 
B - 22.8 
B - 26 
B - 24.3 
```


:::
:::



### Data frames



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
birds <- tibble(species, wing_length)
birds
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 x 2
  species wing_length
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 A              23.1
2 A              25.4
3 B              22.8
4 B              26  
5 B              24.3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
birds |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_wing = mean(wing_length), n = n())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 x 3
  species mean_wing     n
  <chr>       <dbl> <int>
1 A            24.2     2
2 B            24.4     3
```


:::
:::



::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 1
Write a function `classify_mass(x, threshold)` analogous to
`classify_size()` above, returning `"heavy"` or `"light"`. Then create
a `body_mass` vector with 5 values and apply your function to it with
`sapply()`.
:::

## Part 2: Data wrangling

### Import and preview

We'll simulate writing out and reading back a small dataset, since
you won't always start with your own `.csv`. In your own work,
replace this with `read_csv("data/your_file.csv")`.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(42)
growth_wide <- tibble(
  plant_id = 1:12,
  treatment = rep(c("Control", "Fertilizer"), each = 6),
  height_wk1 = round(rnorm(12, 10, 1), 1),
  height_wk2 = round(rnorm(12, 14, 1.5), 1),
  height_wk3 = round(rnorm(12, 18, 2), 1)
)

write_csv(growth_wide, "growth_wide_example.csv")
growth_wide <- read_csv("growth_wide_example.csv")
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
glimpse(growth_wide)
```

### Core dplyr verbs



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
growth_wide |>
  filter(treatment == "Fertilizer") |>
  select(plant_id, height_wk3) |>
  arrange(desc(height_wk3))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 x 2
  plant_id height_wk3
     <dbl>      <dbl>
1        9       20.1
2        8       19.4
3       11       19  
4        7       18.9
5       10       16.8
6       12       14.6
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
growth_wide |>
  mutate(growth_wk1_to_wk3 = height_wk3 - height_wk1) |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(mean_growth = mean(growth_wk1_to_wk3), .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 x 2
  treatment  mean_growth
  <chr>            <dbl>
1 Control           7.4 
2 Fertilizer        6.98
```


:::
:::



### Tidy data: wide → long

Most statistical models in R expect **long/tidy** data — one row per
observation, not one row per subject with repeated-measure columns.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
growth_long <- growth_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("height_wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "height_wk",
    values_to = "height"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.integer(week))

growth_long
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 36 x 4
   plant_id treatment  week height
      <dbl> <chr>     <int>  <dbl>
 1        1 Control       1   11.4
 2        1 Control       2   11.9
 3        1 Control       3   21.8
 4        2 Control       1    9.4
 5        2 Control       2   13.6
 6        2 Control       3   17.1
 7        3 Control       1   10.4
 8        3 Control       2   13.8
 9        3 Control       3   17.5
10        4 Control       1   10.6
# i 26 more rows
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(growth_long, aes(week, height, group = plant_id, color = treatment)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Plant height over time by treatment](week02-tutorial_files/figure-html/fig-growth-1.png){#fig-growth width=672}
:::
:::



### Long → wide



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
growth_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = week, values_from = height, names_prefix = "wk_")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


week 1 height) and identify the plant with the largest total growth
